result: The manuscript establishes the context that age and sex are important biological variables in preclinical mouse studies, but most studies use wide age ranges (4-20 weeks) and do not assess both sexes in parallel, which may negatively impact reproducibility.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C10-C16 collectively establish well-documented problems in preclinical research practices. These claims are supported by multiple citations to published literature and represent established knowledge in the field. The claims accurately describe current practices and their potential consequences.

result: Previous work showed that 4-week-old adolescent mice were more sensitive to innocuous tactile stimulation than 12-week-old adult mice, and these changes correlated with changes in Piezo2 activity and age-dependent transcriptome changes.
evaluation: Claims C17-C18 describe prior published work (Michel et al., 2020) that motivated the current study. These claims are appropriately cited and provide important context for why proteome profiling across ages is needed.

result: Transcript levels show limited correspondence with protein levels, and deep proteome profiling of complex tissues remains challenging, especially for low abundant and transmembrane proteins.
evaluation: Claims C19-C20 represent well-established knowledge in the proteomics field, supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide important justification for conducting proteome-level rather than transcriptome-level analysis.

result: DIA-PASEF offers superior performance for deep proteome profiling compared to DDA-PASEF, and DIA-NN outperforms other DIA data processing software.
evaluation: Claims C21, C74, and C76 describe established technical advantages of the methods used, supported by appropriate citations and direct comparison data shown in Figure 1. The superior performance of DIA-PASEF over DDA-PASEF is demonstrated empirically in this study.

result: DIA-PASEF demonstrated high technical reproducibility with quality control correlations of 0.98-0.99, detected 4135-3926 additional protein groups compared to DDA-PASEF, and showed smaller coefficients of variation.
evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A-F. The high correlations, increased protein identifications, and reduced CVs provide strong evidence for the technical quality and superiority of the DIA-PASEF approach used in this study.

result: The study quantified >8600 protein IDs in paw skin, covering approximately 70% of the most comprehensive human skin proteome, including all 50 known keratins, 19 collagens, 13 interleukin family members, and 11 S100 family members.
evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are supported by data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and 2E. The depth of coverage is impressive and validated by comparison with published human skin proteome data. The identification of complete protein families demonstrates the comprehensiveness of the profiling.

result: The study quantified approximately 8400 protein IDs in SCN, covering 94% of the described myelin proteome (1014/1077 proteins) without myelin enrichment, and robustly quantified multiple ion channels including Trpv1 and voltage-gated sodium channels.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by data shown in Figures 2C, 2D, and 2F. The near-complete coverage of the myelin proteome without enrichment and detection of low-abundance ion channels without membrane preparations demonstrate exceptional depth and quality of the proteomics workflow.

result: Principal component analysis showed that age groups were clearly segregated in both skin and SCN samples, indicating age is a prominent discriminator in the proteome data.
evaluation: Claim C32 is directly supported by PCA plots shown in Figures 2G and 2H. The clear separation of age groups in the PCA provides strong visual and statistical evidence that age is a major source of variation in the proteome data.

result: Age-dependent differential expression analysis revealed 234 and 94 DEPs in female and male skin respectively, with 46 shared DEPs enriched in skin development pathways including protein hydroxylation and collagen fibril organization at 4 weeks, and sex-specific pathway enrichment patterns.
evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are supported by differential expression analysis and pathway enrichment data shown in Figures 3A-D. The statistical criteria (q-value ≤0.05, |log2FC| ≥0.585) are clearly defined, and the biological interpretation of enriched pathways is consistent with known skin development biology.

result: Among 144 DRG ligands and receptors present in the skin dataset, 12 were significantly regulated by age, including Lamb1 which was more abundant in 4-week female skin and Mrc2 which showed age-dependent significance.
evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by comparison with published ligand-receptor interaction data and proteomics results shown in Figure 3E. The identification of age-regulated ligand-receptor pairs provides mechanistic insights into skin-nerve communication during development.

result: Age-dependent comparisons in SCN revealed 929 and 1269 DEPs in female and male mice respectively, with pathway enrichment showing vesicle localization higher at 4 weeks and neuron survival/neurotransmitter transport pathways more pronounced at 14 weeks, and 144 DEPs associated with synapses.
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by differential expression analysis and pathway enrichment data shown in Figures 4A-B and comparison with SynGO database. The large number of age-dependent DEPs (nearly one-fifth of quantified proteome) and their annotation to developmentally relevant pathways provide strong evidence for substantial age-dependent changes in SCN.

result: Among immune cell ligands and glia-neuron ligand-receptor pairs quantified in SCN, 19/56 immune cell ligands and approximately one-third of glia-neuron ligand-receptor pairs showed age-dependent abundance changes.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by comparison with published ligand-receptor interaction databases and proteomics data shown in Figure 4C. The identification of age-dependent changes in cell-cell communication molecules provides important insights into SCN development and maturation.

result: Among myelin proteins, 21/90 were differentially regulated by age, including Mbp and Mpz which were enriched at 14 weeks, Cd59a which was more abundant at adult age, and some myelin DEPs appeared sex-specific (Bcas1, Ca2, Cadm4, Dynll1 in females; Itgb4 in males).
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4D and comparison with published myelin proteome studies. The findings are consistent with known myelin development biology and reveal previously unknown sex-specific differences in myelin protein regulation.

result: Sex-dependent differential expression analysis revealed 58 DEPs in skin and 33 DEPs in SCN within the same age group, with sex-dependent changes much less pronounced at 4 weeks compared to 14 weeks, and no sex-dependent DEPs observed at 4 weeks in SCN.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figures 5A-B. The finding that sex differences are more pronounced at 14 weeks than 4 weeks is consistent with sexual maturation occurring during this developmental window. However, the absence of sex-dependent DEPs at 4 weeks in SCN should be interpreted cautiously given the stringent cutoff criteria used.

result: The pathway 'regulation of complement activation' was significantly enriched in both skin and SCN in sex comparisons at 14 weeks.
evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figures 5E-F. The identification of complement pathway sexual dimorphism in both tissues suggests a conserved sex-dependent immune regulation mechanism.

result: Among 123 sexually dimorphic transcripts from a previous mouse hind paw skin study, 42 proteins were quantified in this dataset, of which 14 were sexually dimorphic at 4 and/or 14 weeks.
evaluation: Claim C61 compares proteome data with published transcriptome data. While 14/42 proteins showed sexual dimorphism consistent with transcriptome data, 28/42 did not. The authors attribute this to the broad age range in the transcriptome study and limited transcript-protein correspondence, which are reasonable explanations. However, the partial concordance limits the strength of validation. The result is uncertain because it's unclear whether the discordance represents true biological differences, technical limitations, or age-matching issues.

result: The skin proteome harbored 329 out of 907 human skin disease genes, of which 27 proteins showed significant age and/or sex dependency across varied skin diseases.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by comparison with skin disease databases shown in Figure 6A. The identification of age/sex-dependent regulation of disease-associated proteins provides translational relevance. However, the comparison between mouse glabrous skin and human hairy skin disease profiles is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

result: Among 841 pain genes, 245 were quantified in the SCN proteome, of which 132 displayed significant age and/or sex-dependent changes, including Ace, Ace2, Fkbp5, and Serpina6 which showed distinct age and sex patterns and are associated with pain susceptibility in humans.
evaluation: Claims C64-C72 are supported by comparison with pain gene databases and proteomics data shown in Figures 6D-F. The identification of age/sex-dependent regulation of pain-associated proteins is well-supported by the data. The connections to human pain susceptibility are appropriately cited. This provides important translational insights for pain research.

result: Several proteins previously reported to be regulated upon spared nerve injury (SNI) in adult males exhibited age-dependent abundance differences in males but not in females in naive mice.
evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by comparison with the authors' previous SNI study data. This finding suggests that baseline age-dependent differences in naive mice may confound interpretation of injury-induced changes, which has important implications for experimental design in pain research. The sex-specific age dependency adds another layer of complexity.

result: The study uncovered significant age and sex differences in mouse paw skin and SCN proteomes, identifying protein subsets and networks correlated with age and/or sex, including proteins and pathways with known pathophysiological relevance such as homeostasis and epidermal signaling in skin, and myelin proteins and regulators of neuronal development in SCN, as well as proteins associated with skin diseases and pain.
evaluation: Claims C4-C9 represent the overarching findings of the study and are supported by the comprehensive proteomics data, differential expression analyses, pathway enrichment analyses, and comparisons with disease databases presented throughout the manuscript. The results are internally consistent and biologically plausible.

result: The current study quantified more than twice as many proteins (~8400 IDs) in SCN compared to a previous study by the same group using DIA-MS (3141 IDs).
evaluation: Claim C75 is supported by comparison with the authors' previous publication. This demonstrates the improved depth of profiling achieved with the DIA-PASEF workflow compared to conventional DIA-MS, validating the technical advancement.

result: The study design analyzed 16 biological replicates of paw skin and SCN samples comparing two age groups (4-week adolescent and 14-week adult) and both sexes in C57BL/6J mice, focusing on tissues involved in nociception, pain, and various pathologies.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 describe the experimental design and rationale. The design is appropriate with adequate biological replicates (n=4 per group after excluding 2 samples). The choice of tissues and age groups is well-justified based on the biological questions and prior literature.

result: The data analysis excluded two samples due to low protein content, applied a 75% quantification threshold across replicates, and used stringent statistical criteria (q-value ≤0.05 and |log2FC| ≥0.585) to identify differentially expressed proteins.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 describe the data analysis criteria. The exclusion of outlier samples is appropriate and transparent. The 75% quantification threshold and statistical cutoffs (including multiple testing correction) are reasonable and clearly defined. However, these stringent criteria mean that some true biological differences may be missed (false negatives), which the authors acknowledge.
